title: The New Math of Law Firm Profitability
author: Gretta Rusanow · Joel Cohen · John Morley

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source shares the cluster’s emphasis on independent judgment and human capabilities, but redirects AI competence away from the law-school curriculum toward workplace training. It favors traditional education and assessment over integrating product-specific AI practice with legal reasoning in school.
qs: We need to think of ourselves as training students not just for the practice of law or not just to produce technically correct answers about the law, but we need to train them in client relations and business and ultimately in leadership and judgment.
I don't think it's terribly useful for us to offer a class on ChatGPT prompts or just teach students how to use Harvey.

st.t: Firm profitability: Revenue growth can hide cost fragility
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s account of why headline revenue or segment labels do not fully explain profitability. It identifies market-share capture, partner investment and higher leverage as mechanisms behind firm-specific growth, while not addressing the cluster’s broader cautions about cost fragility, utilisation, realisation, collections or AI-related pressure.
qs: Rates is one aspect of it, but I think more significantly is you see this outperformance by certain firms in capturing market share and being on a much more aggressive growth trajectory than others in the industry.
They were investing more in leverage to support those partners.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s effects depend on organisational and economic context, then materially extends the cluster by identifying partnership churn as a barrier to owning long-term technology assets and rising specialist and AI-related costs as pressures shaping firm growth. Its report of divergent expectations also reinforces the cluster’s caution that transformation forecasts remain unsettled and qualitative.
qs: I mean, as you know, I talk a lot about the difficulty of law firms in owning long-term hard-to-value assets because of the churn in their partnerships.

And I think that what we're seeing emerge in the industry is, in the case of some firms, perhaps a bit more skepticism about the speed at which generative AI is going to have an impact on the industry than they may have voiced a year ago.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts that AI is more likely to restructure law-firm production and staffing than eliminate lawyers, while stressing that current hiring effects remain unproven. It materially extends the cluster by arguing that costly human and technical implementation may make scale and consolidation increasingly important to firms’ economics.
qs: So there are comp expense pressures, but also implementing generative AI in any meaningful way is going to cost millions and millions of dollars.
I think it will also become an economic imperative for some firms to have a certain, achieve a certain scale to absorb the cost pressures that a generative AI is about to bring.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on selective use-case testing and organisational integration rather than software procurement alone. It materially extends the cluster by connecting implementation to specialised human infrastructure, substantial investment, firm scale, leverage changes and possible consolidation, although these economic effects are presented mainly as predictions rather than measured outcomes.
qs: And then I think there's also a recognition that purchasing the technology is just one piece of it.
Firms are going to have to build a human infrastructure around those tools, right?

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central concern that a more senior, AI-enabled staffing model could weaken the junior-to-expert pipeline. It specifically questions how firms will create experienced mid-level lawyers and continue supplying trained talent to in-house departments if junior intake contracts, while appropriately treating current hiring declines and the value of repetitive junior work as unresolved rather than proven AI effects.
qs: Well, how do you become an experienced mid-level associate if you haven't been a junior associate to begin with?

And it feels like if there are fewer junior associates coming through law firms, that doesn't just affect law firms, it affects the rest of the legal industry because law firms are training grounds and exporters of talent for general councils offices.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s resilience proposition by treating sustained revenue and partner-profit growth as evidence that law firms remain economically durable. Its Am Law-heavy sample limits extrapolation to the entire profession, consistent with the cluster’s warning that elite-firm performance is not universally representative.
qs: The bottom line I think is John, that if I were to look at average annual performance of this industry over the past five years, I mean, you re talking about revenue growth around 8.5%, profits per equity partner tipping over 9.5%, firms have been growing, they ve been investing in their growth over this period of time.
We certainly have the vast majority of the Am Law 100, a good portion of the Am Law second 100, and then we have, as I say, roughly 50 to 55 firms outside of the Am Law 200.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by treating organisational absorption and substantial implementation costs—not software access alone—as immediate constraints, while anticipating a more senior, cylindrical staffing structure and leaving apprenticeship effects unresolved. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that current hiring data do not yet establish AI-driven displacement.
qs: Firms are going to have to build a human infrastructure around those tools, right?
I think what's more likely is that the shape of that leverage will change from the pyramid to more of a cylinder.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious framing: it finds no established AI effect on associate hiring yet, while identifying an emerging shift toward a more senior staffing mix. It does not substantively address the cluster’s proposed responses for preserving apprenticeship or funding development.
qs: I'm likely to see, I think, a more senior mix of associates, a more senior mix of salaried lawyers in general.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s cautious distinction between current evidence and prospective restructuring. It reports no observed AI-driven change in associate hiring, interpreting the recent decline as normalization, while tentatively forecasting a shift from the traditional pyramid toward a more senior, cylinder-shaped staffing model. It does not substantively address training, pricing or buyer pressure.
qs: I've seen a return to historical norms in terms of hiring associates.
I think what's more likely is that the shape of that leverage will change from the pyramid to more of a cylinder.

kp.k: Survey evidence primarily covers larger law firms
kp.d: Rusanow describes Citi's annual survey of over 600 line items, quarterly financial surveys and sentiment surveys covering roughly 200 firms, including roughly 50 to 55 outside the Am Law 200. Financial submissions require senior finance sign-off; AI information comes partly from firm leadership. Participation is voluntary. Although Rusanow presents the results as industry evidence, Morley cautions that visibility into less profitable firms is limited.
qs: So we do a very comprehensive annual survey that collects over 600-odd line items, the revenue drivers of firms, as well as every single expense line item you can imagine.
The most senior finance person needs to sign off on them.
And then some of the generative AI information is coming from the managing partners, the leadership of these firms.
But I think I get the sense that she has less visibility into law firms at the low and middle ends of the spectrum.

kp.k: Strong profitability accompanies increasing market concentration
kp.d: For the preceding five years, Rusanow reports average annual revenue growth around 8.5% and profits per equity partner growth tipping over 9.5%, despite post-pandemic volatility. She reports demand growth of 1.6% for the industry versus more than 3.5% for the top 15 over that period, linking outperformance to investment in partners and supporting leverage. Larger firms have gained market share, but she emphasizes that highly profitable branded firms also exist outside the largest rankings.
qs: revenue growth around 8.5%, profits per equity partner tipping over 9.5%
if the industry as a whole saw demand go up 1.6% over the last five years, the top 15 saw an increase of more than 3.5%.
They were investing more in leverage to support those partners.
We certainly see highly successful firms across all segments of the market.

kp.k: Growth strategies emphasize laterals and client-aligned expertise
kp.d: Rusanow reports headcount growth of roughly 2.5% over the preceding five years versus around 1.5%, or the high ones, before the pandemic. With modest overall billable-hours growth, firms pursue lateral recruitment to capture competitors' work. She argues that profitability depends on considered expansion aligned with existing clients, rather than scale alone, and expects smaller-firm acquisitions and laterals to remain more prevalent than difficult mega mergers.
qs: the headcount growth overall for the last five years has been roughly 2.5%.
firms recognize that in order to outperform, they need to be not just growing organically, but also growing through laterals.
size doesn't necessarily translate into profitability.
It's a lot easier to do more with your existing clients than to bring on new practices and then go out to market and try and find new clients.

kp.k: Transactional dependence introduces volatility and collection delays
kp.d: Rusanow reports a shift toward transactional practices that has improved profitability for some firms while increasing exposure to market fluctuations. Transactional payments may await deal completion, unlike the monthly payment pattern she associates with litigation; stalled deals therefore lengthen collection cycles. This is an existing business-model pressure, not an observed AI effect.
qs: I think we've seen a much greater shift toward transactional in the process.
If a deal is frozen because no one can settle on the price or for any number of reasons, the payment to firms just has to wait until the deal closes.
Whereas under the litigation model, you tend to get paid on a monthly basis.

kp.k: Specialist professional roles increase firms' operating costs
kp.d: Rusanow describes declining professional-staff-to-lawyer ratios, particularly secretarial staffing, beginning before the pandemic and accelerating during it. More complex firms have simultaneously recruited higher-paid business development, pricing, project management, technology and data science personnel. She connects these changes to growing expense pressure and the need to integrate expertise across expanding firms.
qs: the trend for a number of years was to reduce the ratio of professional staff to lawyers, particularly secretarial staff.
pricing specialists and project managers and technology people, now you've got data scientists coming into the mix.
all of these people are at much higher salaries than the secretaries who were let go.

kp.k: Firm leaders diverge on AI's competitive significance
kp.d: Rusanow reports divergent leadership views rather than demonstrated AI outcomes: some firms have become more skeptical about the speed of change and await established legal vendors' product suites, while others invest heavily in AI as a transformational differentiator. She recalls substantial tool-assessment work a year to a year and a half earlier, with uneven product maturity. Morley subsequently predicts that this strategic divergence will produce winners and losers.
qs: perhaps a bit more skepticism about the speed at which generative AI is going to have an impact on the industry than they may have voiced a year ago.
the former are more likely to wait for one of the big legal vendors to come up with a suite of products.
some of them absolutely believe that this is going to be a game changer and are investing heavily in it, and believe it's going to give them a competitive edge.
That divergence will probably create some winners and some losers.

kp.k: Hiring declines do not yet establish AI displacement
kp.d: Asked whether AI is already affecting associate hiring strategy, Rusanow says she is not seeing it yet. Citi's research found first-year and summer associate hiring in 25 below 24, but she characterizes 24 as anomalous and the subsequent level as a return to historical norms. She nevertheless sees preliminary indications of a more senior associate and salaried-lawyer mix, distinguishing that signal from evidence of AI-driven hiring reductions.
qs: We're not seeing it yet.
We just did some research on first year and summer associate hiring trends in 25. The numbers were lower than the prior year, 24.
But when I look at the longer term trend, 24 was actually the anomaly.
I've seen a return to historical norms in terms of hiring associates.
I'm likely to see, I think, a more senior mix of associates, a more senior mix of salaried lawyers in general.

kp.k: AI may reshape rather than shrink leverage
kp.d: Rusanow predicts a shift from pyramidal staffing toward a cylinder with more experienced lawyers, rather than necessarily fewer non-equity fee earners relative to equity partners. She reports a quarter of large firms expecting leverage-model changes by 2027 and something like 63% expecting changes sometime between two and 10 years. These are leadership expectations, not observed staffing outcomes; respondents anticipate more strategic advisory work and greater demand for technology and project skills.
qs: I think what's more likely is that the shape of that leverage will change from the pyramid to more of a cylinder.
You've already got a quarter of large firms telling us they expect to make changes to their leverage model just by 2027.
that's gone up to something like 63% of large firms believe that sometime between two and 10 years, there'll be a change.
They believe that there'll be more demand for more strategic advisory work done by lawyers who are more tech savvy with better project skills as well.

kp.k: Cylindrical staffing creates training and retention dilemmas
kp.d: Rusanow questions how firms will produce experienced associates if fewer juniors enter. The hosts extend this concern to law firms' role supplying trained lawyers to corporate legal departments. Rusanow and Morley speculate that higher retention needs could improve advancement prospects. In their closing discussion, the hosts leave unresolved whether automation removes essential formative tasks or lets associates develop higher-level skills sooner.
qs: Well, how do you become an experienced mid-level associate if you haven't been a junior associate to begin with?
law firms are training grounds and exporters of talent for general councils offices.
But in a more cylindrical model, you hire fewer associates, but you have to retain a higher percentage of them.

One thought is that associates will lose out on the opportunity to do the entry level tasks that help them build higher level skills. Another thought maybe is that they just go straight to developing higher level skills.

kp.k: Legal education should emphasize judgment over tool-specific training
kp.d: Morley argues that Yale should teach client relations, business, leadership and judgment rather than merely technically correct legal answers. He regards prompting and Harvey training as better delivered on the job and coding as outside the school's core strength. He also anticipates greater use of handwritten examinations as generative AI complicates assessment, while acknowledging Yale graduates' relatively insulated employment position.
qs: we need to train them in client relations and business and ultimately in leadership and judgment.
I don't think it's terribly useful for us to offer a class on ChatGPT prompts or just teach students how to use Harvey.
Those are things that are best taught on the job.
I do think paradoxically, we're going to see more blue books as the world becomes more technological.

kp.k: AI implementation requires costly organizational change
kp.d: Rusanow predicts meaningful generative AI implementation will cost millions and require scale, potentially accelerating consolidation as an economic necessity. Beyond purchasing software, firms must test use cases, recruit technology, data science and knowledge-management specialists, and embed tools into everyday practice. She expressly declines to claim authoritative knowledge of application maturity, distinguishing longstanding AI in e-discovery from potential generative AI applications in transactional due diligence.
qs: implementing generative AI in any meaningful way is going to cost millions and millions of dollars.
I actually also think that's going to be a driver of continued consolidation in the market as those expense pressures become even more aggressive.
Firms are going to have to build a human infrastructure around those tools, right?
Figuring out ways to have lawyers evolve from seeing it as a shiny new novelty to actually inculcating it in the way they practice law every single day.
In all honesty, I don't feel that I'm as close enough to it to speak with any great authority.

kp.k: Income partnerships primarily serve competitive talent retention
kp.d: Rusanow attributes growing income, or non-equity, partnerships primarily to retaining senior talent and providing a partner title with which to build an equity-worthy practice, rather than protecting equity profits. Newly adopting firms generally treat the role as a transitional stage. She reports carefully managed net equity-partner numbers and increasing leverage through income partners, while noting that some firms retain counsel tracks and others replace them.
qs: Most of the focus has been on growing leverage.
it's not driven by a desire to protect equity.
For the most part, where firms are introducing this for the first time, it is very much as the model of the way station to equity.
It's talent retention, that's exactly what it is.
in certain industries they need to have a partner title to be taken seriously.

kp.k: Income-partner economics depend on productivity and credible progression
kp.d: Under Citi's contribution-per-timekeeper calculation—revenue less compensation and allocated overhead—Rusanow says income partners contribute less on average than counsel or associates, though not necessarily negatively today. Historically, highly paid former equity partners with declining practices could generate less revenue than their compensation. She warns that poorly managed income-partner tracks can undermine motivation, morale and progression for others; the increasing seniority of leverage also raises expenses.
qs: the economics of having a two-tier partnership only work when you have a highly motivated, highly productive group of income partners.
They might not be, they might not necessarily be negative, but they're not, they are not contributing as much as Council or Associates.
I'm calculating what revenue they're generating, and then I'm subtracting their expense to the firm, both comp expense and overhead allocation.
And then it becomes a blocker to people behind them as well.

kp.d: Rusanow describes refinement rather than wholesale reversal of international strategy: firms have scaled back China investment since before the pandemic and reduced exposure to Europe, while prioritizing London and transatlantic growth and considering targeted opportunities such as the UAE. A host suggests remote work may reduce the need for physical offices, but Rusanow explicitly says she has not studied that connection closely.
qs: I don't think it's a cut and dry as growing more or a reversal, so much as a refinement of their international strategy.
They've been scaling back from that investment for several years now, even pre-pandemic.
when you talk about international strategy for firms, it is first and foremost London.
It's actually not something I've looked at particularly closely

kp.k: Outside investment remains uneven and jurisdiction-dependent
kp.d: Rusanow reports more private equity activity outside the US, particularly under UK alternative business structure legislation, alongside interest in law-firm back-office service companies. She identifies US state-level ownership restrictions as obstacles and observes investment in high street firms that provides scale for AI adoption. Morley argues that long-permitted outside ownership has not displaced traditional firms at the top of the UK corporate market; Rusanow agrees it has not penetrated Biglaw but predicts mounting expenses could strengthen incentives.
qs: At the moment, I'm seeing more activity outside of the US, I think, particularly in the UK, where the alternative business legislation has enabled non-lawyer ownership for quite some time, the ABS legislation.
We've seen some interest in private equity investment in the service companies of firms.
the private equity firms who are investing in high street law firms and are giving them effectively the scale needed to be able to adopt generative AI.
I do think that there are a number of market forces that are making it a much more compelling topic than it has been over the last 20 years.

kp.k: External AI suppliers may capture legal-sector value
kp.d: Morley predicts that AI technology will mainly originate outside law firms, which will purchase it, shifting some legal-sector value toward conventionally investor-financed businesses. He nevertheless expects firms' worker-owned model to persist for quite some time. This is his forecast, not a Citi finding; the hosts also discuss a reported Cleary acquisition of an AI technology company as a surprising example of firm ownership of technology.
qs: I think that AI technology is gonna come mainly from outside of law firms
which will shift some of the value in the legal services industry outside of law firms to other elements.
And those other elements of the legal sector will be financed by investors in the same manner as conventional businesses.
I do think law firms will continue to exist in basically their current worker-owned model for quite some time.

kp.k: Consolidation need not eliminate strong smaller firms
kp.d: Rusanow expects continued consolidation and larger firms growing at smaller firms' expense, driven jointly by modest demand growth and accelerating cost pressures, including AI adoption. She nevertheless predicts continuing demand for high-quality branded smaller firms. The hosts conclude that the high end remains healthy rather than facing imminent collapse, while expressly withholding that conclusion for less visible low- and middle-profitability segments.
qs: the larger firms will grow at the expense of smaller firms.
But at the same time, I think that there'll still be a demand for high quality brand smaller firms as well.
So, I don't think that we're going to see the end of small firms.
I don't really know how healthy that segment of the industry is. But certainly at the high end, it is an incredibly healthy industry.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gretta Rusanow predicts changes to staffing composition, substantial implementation costs and cost-driven consolidation, while reporting divergent expectations among firms about AI's speed and competitive significance.
pts.d: Rusanow reports that some firms have become more skeptical about how quickly generative AI will affect legal practice and are more inclined to await established legal vendors' product suites. Others regard AI as potentially transformative and are investing to differentiate themselves; these are reported leadership expectations, not demonstrated competitive outcomes. She says Citi is not yet seeing AI affect associate hiring strategy: lower first-year and summer associate hiring in 2025 than in 2024 represents a return to historical norms rather than evidence of AI-driven cuts. Nevertheless, she sees early indications of a more senior mix of associates and salaried lawyers and predicts a shift from a pyramid toward a cylinder, rather than necessarily a reduction in leverage. Meaningful AI implementation, she argues, will cost millions of dollars and require human infrastructure as well as software, creating a need for scale and helping drive consolidation. She also identifies private equity investment in high street firms as a means of providing the scale needed for AI adoption. Her consolidation prediction does not imply the disappearance of high-quality, branded smaller firms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of Citi hiring research, surveys of firm leaders and Rusanow's advisory conversations; quantified staffing expectations are not measured AI effects.
pts.d: Rusanow describes Citi's broader research infrastructure as annual financial surveys covering more than 600 line items, quarterly flash surveys and sentiment surveys, drawing on over 200 firms. The broader sample is concentrated in the AmLaw 200, with roughly 50–55 firms outside it; the transcript does not specify the sample size or methodology of each AI-related survey. Financial submissions usually come from CFOs or executive directors, whereas some generative-AI information comes from managing partners and firm leadership. The principal quantified AI-related evidence is that a quarter of large firms expect leverage-model changes by 2027 and approximately 63% anticipate changes within a two-to-ten-year horizon. Those percentages describe expectations, not observed changes or an estimate of AI's causal contribution. Her reading of 2025 hiring draws on research into first-year and summer associate trends, but no hiring counts or AI attribution analysis are supplied. Claims about competitive differentiation, multimillion-dollar costs, consolidation and private-equity-enabled adoption rest on professional observations and economic reasoning, without named transactions, itemized costs, productivity benchmarks or measured returns. Her discussion of applications distinguishes longstanding AI use in e-discovery from potential generative-AI use in transactional due diligence and explicitly limits her own technical authority.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Near-term hiring observations are separated from forecasts for 2027 and the following decade; competitive and consolidation effects depend on adoption, implementation and firms' differing strategies.
pts.d: In this source labeled 2026, Rusanow compares 2025 hiring with 2024 and describes changing AI sentiment relative to a year or a year and a half earlier. She reports that firms previously spent considerable time assessing tools with uneven maturity, many of which they considered not yet market-ready. Current expectations remain divided, so she does not give a uniform date for transformation. Leverage-model survey responses cover changes by 2027 and a broader two-to-ten-year horizon. Her own cylindrical-staffing forecast is qualified as more likely, not inevitable; firms are not uniformly convinced that leverage will shrink. Cost and consolidation predictions concern meaningful implementation and increasing adoption, not software purchase alone. She argues that successful deployment requires supporting personnel, use-case testing and changes to everyday legal practice. She gives no precise timetable for cost-driven consolidation or wider private equity involvement and acknowledges that investor ownership has not penetrated BigLaw in the way under discussion.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects concern firms' scale and expenses, junior-to-senior lawyer career pathways, demand for strategically and technologically capable lawyers, and supporting professional roles.
pts.d: For firms, AI adds expenditure and organizational requirements that Rusanow expects to favor sufficient scale, including growth or consolidation; private-equity-backed high street firms are a specific example of smaller practices gaining adoption capacity. For associates and other salaried lawyers, the projected change is toward greater seniority rather than necessarily fewer non-partner lawyers per partner. Fewer juniors alongside stronger demand for experienced associates would create a training-pipeline problem. Rusanow also tentatively suggests that a cylindrical structure could improve an associate's chance of reaching equity partnership. She reports firms expecting greater demand for strategic advisory work performed by lawyers with stronger technology and project skills, raising questions for law schools about preparation. Data scientists, technology personnel and knowledge-management specialists form part of the additional human infrastructure she considers necessary for successful adoption. Her claims primarily concern provider-side organization and careers; she supplies no concrete estimate of client savings or access-to-justice effects.
